title: Tithing begins with surplus, then a tenth of yearly increase
setting: Joseph Smith dictated this revelation at Far West, Missouri, on 8 July 1838. He had asked how much of the Saints’ property the Lord required as tithing. At that time “tithing” meant any donation to Church funds, not a set tenth. The Church carried heavy debt from the Kirtland Temple, failed Ohio ventures, and the Panic of 1837. The Saints also needed money to build up their Missouri settlements.
summary: The revelation asks the Saints to give all their surplus property to the bishop in Zion. The funds are for the temple, the foundation of Zion, the priesthood, and the Presidency’s debts. This first gift is called “the beginning of the tithing”. After that, members are to pay one-tenth of their interest each year. The revelation calls this “a standing law” forever. Those who gather to Zion must keep it, or they will not be worthy to stay. If the people do not keep it, the land will not be Zion to them. The law is to be an example for all the stakes.

contextNote.title: One-tenth of interest, after the surplus
contextNote.text: Joseph Smith asked how much property the Lord required, and verses 1–4 answer in two steps. First, verse 1 asks for all surplus property, given once to the bishop. Then verse 4 sets an ongoing rule of “one-tenth of all their interest annually”. A Joseph Smith Papers note explains surplus as property the owner could not put to good use. Church leaders have long read “interest” as a person’s yearly increase or income. In this passage, tithing is a yearly tenth of increase built on an earlier one-time gift.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 115–120 discusses this law of tithing. According to verses 6–7, what does keeping this law do for the land of Zion and its stakes?
reviewNote: Read all 7 verses. Official heading gives Far West, 8 July 1838, Joseph's question, and the earlier broad meaning of tithing. JSP historical introduction read for the financial background, the December 1837 two-percent proposal, presidency debts, and the surplus footnote. Edward Partridge is the bishop in Zion (v. 1), not named in the text. The reading of interest as income reflects later Church usage and is attributed as such.
